passage: When the panchayat clerk announced that the school-book printing order had gone to Arohi's press, Hansa felt her jaw set. Two years in the same lane, and Arohi always seemed to get the luck. On the bus home she muttered to the conductor that Arohi must have greased somebody, then stopped, hearing herself. Nobody had said any such thing. The next morning she went to the clerk instead and asked, politely, why her bid had not been chosen. "The sample page and the delivery date," he said. "Arohi printed a sample overnight and brought it." Hansa looked at her own quote folder, all price and no sample. She wrote in her notebook: bring a sample, promise a date, keep it. Then she walked down the lane and, without gushing, told Arohi congratulations.

qa.q: Why did the panchayat clerk say Hansa's bid was not chosen?
qa.a: He said it came down to the sample page and the delivery date, since Arohi printed a sample overnight and brought it.

qa.q: What did Hansa realise when she heard herself muttering on the bus?
qa.a: She realised her envy was making her accuse Arohi of something nobody had said, so she stopped.

qa.q: What did Hansa do to turn envy into improvement?
qa.a: She asked the clerk why the bid was lost, noted to bring a sample and promise a date, and congratulated Arohi instead of bad-mouthing.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Hansa's congratulations?
qa.a: Arohi may be pleasantly surprised and see Hansa as a fair rival, especially since Hansa's grumbling on the bus never reached Arohi.

grounding: Hansa loses a bid and feels envy of the rival, then asks what the rival did better, plans to improve and does not run the rival down.
